prayer.text: Saint Katharine Drexel, pray for us.

cues.text: Heiress to a Banking Fortune
Born on November 26, 1858, in Philadelphia, Katharine Drexel was the second daughter of the financier Francis Anthony Drexel.
Her mother died only five weeks after her birth, and Katharine and her older sister were first raised by an aunt and uncle.
In 1860, their father remarried Emma Bouvier, a devout and generous stepmother who welcomed both girls as her own.
The Drexel household combined considerable wealth with an unusually active practice of charity.
Three days each week, the family opened its own home to distribute food, clothing, and rent assistance to Philadelphia’s poor.
This taught Katharine the ordinary duty of almsgiving long before she ever imagined a religious vocation.
An Awakening to a Nation's Need
Educated by private tutors, Katharine traveled widely through the United States and Europe with her sisters.
During trips through the American West, she grew increasingly troubled by the poverty and neglect she witnessed among Native American communities.
She was also troubled by the corresponding hardships facing Black Americans in the postwar South.
Her father's death in 1885 left the three Drexel sisters an immense fortune.
Still only in her twenties, Katharine began quietly funding missions and schools for both communities before settling on any more direct form of personal service.
An Audience That Redirected a Life

In 1887, Katharine and her sisters traveled to Rome and were received in a private audience by Pope Leo XIII , whom she asked to send additional missionaries to staff the Native American missions she was already funding.
The pope's reply, by her own later account, redirected the whole course of her life: he asked her, simply, why she did not become a missionary herself.

Under the spiritual direction of Bishop James O'Connor of Omaha, Katharine spent the following years discerning this call with real seriousness, eventually resolving to found a new religious congregation rather than join an existing one.
Renouncing a Fortune for Religious Life
Katharine entered religious formation with the Sisters of Mercy in 1889.
On February 12, 1891, she professed her vows alongside thirteen companions.
She became the first member of a new community, the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament for Indians and Colored People.
She devoted the great majority of her considerable inheritance — some twenty million dollars over the course of her lifetime — to funding the new congregation's missions.
She understood her wealth not as a possession to be enjoyed, but as a trust to be spent entirely in service of those American society had most thoroughly overlooked.
Building Schools Across a Divided Nation
Over more than four decades as superior of her growing congregation, Mother Katharine established and staffed missions and schools across the United States.

These served Native American and Black communities, from a boarding school for Pueblo children in New Mexico to St. Michael's School on the Navajo reservation and dozens of institutions throughout the segregated South.
In 1925, she founded Xavier University in New Orleans.
It remains to this day the only Catholic historically Black university in the country—a monument to her lifelong conviction that quality education was a matter of justice owed, not charity bestowed.
Final Years
A serious heart attack in 1935 forced Katharine to step back from active governance of her congregation.

She spent her remaining two decades in a quieter life of prayer at the motherhouse in Bensalem, Pennsylvania, continuing to write letters of encouragement to her sisters and intercede for missions she could no longer visit in person.
She died there on March 3, 1955, at ninety-six years old, having given to the poor of two racial communities in America not merely her fortune but the greater part of her own life.
Legacy
Katharine Drexel was beatified in 1988 and canonized on October 1, 2000, by Pope John Paul II, becoming the second person born in the United States to be raised to the altars of the Church.
Honored today as patroness of racial justice and of philanthropists, she remains a model of a truth the Gospel has always taught.
The modern world still finds it difficult to practice: that real wealth, rightly understood, is measured not by what is kept.
It is measured by how completely, and how patiently, it is given away.
